title: Iron-doping on Cu–N–C composite with enhanced CO faraday efficiency for the electrochemical reduction of CO2
abstract: Fe–N–macrocycles have been viewing as the most promising catalyst for CO2ER. It is of great importance to explore the performance of composite CuFe–N–C in CO2ER. Fe-Cu–BTT precursor was prepared by introducing the ferrous ion to a microporous N-rich MOF. It exhibits a lower plateau temperature of 800 °C than the prototype. The pyrolysis product of FexCu–N–C increases the selectivity of CO2-to− CO due to the increase of the BET surface area, the total pore volume, and the Fe–Nx sites, as well as a lower density of Cu NPs in the carbon matrix. The Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 exhibits the highest FECO of 48.5 %.

Iron-doping on Cu–N–C composite with enhanced CO faraday efficiency for the electrochemical reduction of CO2
Si-Min Cao 1, Hua-Bo Chen 1, Meng-Jie Liu , Bao-Qi Feng , Bao-Xia Dong *, Qiu-Hui Zheng , Wen-Long Liu , Yun-Lei Teng * School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Yangzhou University, Yangzhou, 225002, Jiangsu, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Carbon monoxide Metal-organic framework Copper nanoparticle Iron Nitrogen-rich
A B S T R A C T
Fe–N–macrocycles have been viewing as the most promising catalyst for CO2ER. It is of great importance to explore the performance of composite CuFe–N–C in CO2ER. Fe-Cu–BTT precursor was prepared by introducing the ferrous ion to a microporous N-rich MOF. It exhibits a lower plateau temperature of 800 ℃ than the prototype. The pyrolysis product of FexCu–N–C increases the selectivity of CO2-to− CO due to the increase of the BET surface area, the total pore volume, and the Fe–Nx sites, as well as a lower density of Cu NPs in the carbon matrix. The Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 exhibits the highest FECO of 48.5 %.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
In the past few years, the electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2ER) into high-energy liquid or gas fuels as a way to store intermittent energy has gained intense attention. Due to the inertia of CO2 and the fact that the process requires multiple-electron and proton transfers to be converted, its practical application remains a significant challenge [1,2]. The high over-potential of the reaction and the low activity of existing catalysts still prevent the process from approaching comercialization.
At present, it is urgent to develop high-efficient catalysts and find appropriate reaction conditions (such as solvent, temperature, pressure, etc.) to effectively promote the transfer of electrons/protons, inhibit the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and ensure the high selectivity of catalysts [3–5]. Cu is the only known catalyst capable of conversion of CO2 into hydrocarbons with a reasonably high Faraday efficiency (FE). Both experimental and theoretical studies (i.e., focus on the key intermediates, different reaction pathways, etc.) are devoted to improving the over-potential and selectivity of CO2ER over copper catalysts [6–8]. Bimetallic catalysts have shown the capability to turn the binding strength of key intermediates due to the electronic and geometric effects produced by alloying, therefore tune its CO2ER catalytic activity and selectivity [9]. In this context, Cu-based alloys such as Cu–Co, Cu–Ni, Cu–Ag, Cu–Ru, Cu–Pd, Cu–Au, have been investigated [10–14]. Since Fe is one of the most earth-abundant metals, the alloying element of Fe in Cu-based alloys has remained undeveloped.
Many researchers found that the N-doped C-supported transition metals, i.e., M–N–C, have unusual catalytic activity for the CO2ER, due to that it has a similar active site to M–N–macrocycles and their advantages of low cost, adjustable specific surface [15–18]. In consideration that Fe–N–macrocycles have been viewing as the most promising catalyst for CO2ER, it is of great importance to explore the performance of composite CuFe–N–C in CO2ER [19].
Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are a kind of porous inorganic materials with a high specific surface area. When using it as the precursor, it could achieve a good dispersion of metal ions due to its uniform arrangement of the crystal lattice [20]. Pyrolyzing MOFs is a relatively simple and straightforward method to prepare functional porous hybrid materials of metal/metal oxide–C [21–27]. HKUST-1 and ZIF-8 are two types of models in this subject [17,22,26,22–27]. A nitrogen-rich (37.4 %) precursor of 3D rigid MOF Cu–BTT ([Cu(DMF)6] [(Cu4Cl)3(BTT)8(H2O)12], H3BTT = 1,3,5-benzenetristetrazolate; DMF= N, N-dimethylformamide) has been employed in our group, which guarantee the one-step preparation of Cu–N–C material [28]. Well-dispersed Cu nanoparticles (20–40 nm) in the N-rich carbon matrix were obtained under different pyrolysis temperatures, i.e., Cu–N–CT (T = 600–1100 ◦C), among which the Cu–N–C1100 exhibits the highest FE for CO2ER product (FECO =40.8 % and FEHCOOH = 38.1 %).
In this work, the ferrous ion with different contents was introduced to the precursor Cu–BTT for obtaining Fe-Cu–BTT and pyrolysis products of FexCu–N–C. The presence of ferrous ions in the precursor lowers

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis of FexCu–BTT
sections.text: H3BTT ligand was synthesized followed a similar process as reported [29]. A certain mass of CuCl2⋅2H2O, FeCl2⋅4H2O, and 142.0 mg H3BTT was dissolved in 32.0 mL DMF to obtain the yellow-green suspension. The mole amount of FeCl2⋅4H2O was kept at 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 mmol, respectively, and the total amount of CuCl2⋅2H2O and FeCl2⋅4H2O was maintained at 1.6 mmol. The suspension was stirred at room temperature for 30 min to disperse it evenly. The solution was then placed in a 100 mL Teflon reactor and heated for 12 h at 120 ℃. Wash the product with DMF 3 times and dry it in the air. According to the different reaction doses, the obtained precursors were labeled as Fe0.3Cu–BTT, Fe0.5Cu–BTT, and Fe0.8Cu–BTT.

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis of FexCu–N–C800 composite catalyst
sections.text: The FexCu–BTT precursor was placed in a furnace, heated to 800 ℃ at 3 ℃ min–1 heating rate under an argon condition, and kept constant for 1 h. Combining with the ICP results (Table S1), the obtained composites were named as Fe0.01Cu–N–C800, Fe0.07Cu–N–C800, and Fe0.13Cu–N–C800, respectively, based on the Fe: Cu ratios.

sections.heading: 3.1. Characterizations of FexCu–BTT and FexCu–N–C800
sections.text:
X-ray powder diffraction patterns (PXRD) of FexCu–BTT exhibit a similar diffraction peak with that of Cu–BTT and the simulated one, indicating the structure keeps intact after the introduction of Fe2+
(Fig. 1a). The TG-DSC curves for FexCu–BTT reaches the plateau at a lower temperature of 800 ℃, substantially lower than 1000 ℃, which is required for Cu–BTT (Fig. S1). Herein, we choose 800 ℃ as the pyrolysis temperature for obtaining the derived material. After the carbonization, the framework loses the solvent molecule and the unstable C and N. As shown in Fig. 1b, the crystalline Cu contributes most to each product, exhibiting diffraction peaks at 2θ = 43.30◦, 50.43◦, and 74.13◦, respectively, which are attributed to the crystal faces of (111), (200) and (220). As the increase of the content of Fe, diffraction peaks belonging to the crystal plane of Fe(110) at 2θ = 44.67◦ were gradually distinct, especially in Fe0.07Cu–N–C800, and Fe0.13Cu–N–C800 (Table S2).
Further analysis of the diffraction peak intensity of each crystal plane indicates that the introduction of Fe leads to the increase of Cu(111) and Cu(200), and a decrease of Cu(220). An except is observed in Fe0.01Cu–N–C800 that the intensity of Cu(220) increases. The intensity ratios for the (111)/(200), (111)/(220), and (200)/(220) are all the highest in Fe0.07Cu–N–C800, hinting at the prominent of Cu(111) and Cu (200) crystal planes after the introduction of Fe. Moreover, the FWHM (full width at half maximum) for all the diffraction peaks of Cu reduces gradually as the Fe content increase, indicating the crystallite size increases progressively.

Fig. S2 exhibits the SEM images of the FexCu–N–C800 catalyst samples. The coral reef morphology in pristine Cu–N–C800 (the pyrolysis product from Cu–BTT at 800 ℃) disappears gradually after the Fedoping due to the melting and agglomerating of the particles. Larger pores are left as a result. The corresponding EDS results proved that all elements of Fe, Cu, C, and N are uniformly dispersed (Fig. S3).
To evaluate the effect of Fe-doping on the surface area and pore distribution of the composite materials, nitrogen adsorption and desorption tests were carried out, as shown in Fig. 2. The Fe-doped catalysts all exhibit higher Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area and total pore volume compared with the undoped one (Table S3, 164 m2 g–1 and 0.17 cm3 g–1 for Cu–N–C800). Among them, the
Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 catalyst increases the most in the total pore volume (0.55 cm3 g–1), especially in the range of 30–120 nm (0.48 cm3 g–1), which is vital for the electron transfer and mass transport in catalysis reaction (Fig. 2b). As is well known, having a larger BET surface area will be propitious to adsorb CO2 and release the intermediate. It, therefore, prevents the accumulation of bubbles on the surface of the electrode. Bubbles on the electrode are undesirable because they will cause the peel off of the catalyst and lead to a short life of it. Therefore, the introduction of Fe induced a change of the structure, causing the raise of the total pore volume and surface area, which would probably improve the selectivity of the catalyst.
Notably, it does not cause an apparent change in the morphology of the composite catalyst, as shown in the TEM images (Fig. S4). The Cu and Fe NPs are co-existing in the composite catalysts with a size around 28 ± 2 nm, as indicated by the acid treatment result (Fig. S5). The solution color changes from grey to deep yellow, verifying the existence of Fe2+ in the solution after the treatment.
The Raman spectra present the graphitization degree of each catalyst (Fig. 3). The IG/ID (G represents the graphitized carbon around 1593 cm− 1; D denotes the defective carbon at 1353 cm− 1) intensity ratio indicates that the addition of Fe induces a higher degree of graphitization, hinting that the electron transfer will be facilitated through the implantation [30].
We conducted XPS tests on the samples to obtain the valence states of each element in the FexCu–N–C800 material (Fig. 4). The strong signals at 932.30 eV (Cu 2p3/2) and 952.60 eV (Cu 2p1/2) indicate the presence of Cu◦ (Fig. 4b) [31]. The characteristic peak of CuII at 933.40 eV was also observed, accompany a weak satellite peak in the high-energy region in Fe0.01Cu–N–C800. With the increase of Fe content, the spectral lines of Cu 2p and N 1s are all shifted to the direction of high binding energy

(Fig. 4b,c), and the characteristic peak for CuII gradually weakened, hinting that the content of CuII declined [32]. Therefore, we conclude that the main existing form is Cu◦ in Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 and Fe0.13Cu–N–C800.
In combination with the identification convention of typical M–N–C materials, we divide the N species into five groups, that is, pyridine N, Nx–M/amine N, pyrrole N, graphite N/quaternary N, and NO [33,34]. The corresponding binding energy is centered at 398.06, 399.45, 400.52 ± 0.3, 402.23, and 402.23 eV, respectively. From the XPS analysis, we can observe that total N content in FexCu–N–C800 material decreases as the increase of Fe content, which keeps pace with the results of CHN element analysis (Table S4–S5). The pyrrole N, pyridine N, and M–Nx contribute most to the total N, while the pyridine N and M–Nx decreased as the increase of Fe (Fig. S6). The iron species are existed mainly in the form of Fe2+ (711.23 eV 2p3/2 and the satellite peak at 720.18 eV; 725.22 eV 2p1/2) and Fe3+ (715.57 eV 2p3/2, 727.86 eV 2p1/2 and the satellite peak at 733.46 eV) [35]. No detectable signal for metallic iron around 706.7 eV is found in each spectrum, suggesting that the content of Fe◦ is low. Evidenced from XPS analysis, the introduced Fe in FexCu–N–C800 material is mainly presented in the form of Fe–Nx. Since the content of CuII (3d9) is low and the d-orbital of Cu◦ is fully occupied, we speculate that the coordinate covalent bonds between copper and nitrogen are inhibited as the addition of Fe [36,37]. Moreover, a higher Fe atomic percentage is observed in Fe0.07Cu-N-C800 than that of Fe0.13Cu-N-C800 based on the XPS analysis. We speculate that the metal NPs are tightly wrapped in the carbon layer due to the melting after the Fe doping, among which the Fe0.13Cu-N-C800 suffered from agglomeration the most serious (Fig. S2). Since XPS is a typical surface analysis technique, only a thin layer of photoelectrons near the sample’s surface can escape and be detected. Therefore, metal NPs wrapped in the carbon layer may not be accurately detected.

sections.heading: 3.2.1. Linear voltammetry
sections.text: Linear volt-ampere (LSV) test was carried out in N2-/CO2- saturated electrolyte solution to preliminary explore the CO2ER performance of the synthetic FexCu–N–C800 (Fig. 5). All FexCu–N–C800 catalysts showed a higher cathodic current density in the CO2-saturated solution than that in the N2-saturated one, indicating that they exhibit the catalytic role toward the reduction of CO2. Moreover, at the same potential and the same electrolyte solution (CO2-saturated), the FexCu–N–C800 catalysts exhibit a higher current density than Cu–N–C800, hinting that Fe promotes the catalytic reduction of CO2 reaction.

sections.heading: 3.2.2. Chronoamperometry
sections.text:
To explore the selectivity of the catalyst for CO2ER, we tested the time-current curves of various materials from –1.1 to –1.6 V vs. Ag/AgCl in a gas-tight H-type cell (Fig. 6). Much higher total current densities were found in the Fe-doped catalysts. Gaseous CO and H2, and liquidphase of formic acid were detected as the main products through gas chromatography (by thermal conductivity detector) and ion chromatography, respectively. The FE of each product was calculated based on the quantification results through the standard lines (Fig. S7–S8). For possible alcohols, acetone, and hydrocarbon products, a flame ionization detector was employed for detection. No such product was found (Fig. S9). The FE-potential relationship for each catalyst is shown in Fig. 7. It is found that the addition of Fe inhibits the generation of H2 and HCOOH, and facilitates the production of CO. For the Cu–N–C800 catalyst, FEH2, FEHCOOH, and FECO maintain in the range of 63.0–72.5 %, 11.2~22.1, and 5.4–13.1 %, respectively. The FEH2 is inhibited remarkably in the potential scope of –1.1 ~ –1.4 V vs. Ag/AgCl after doping of Fe, and sometimes as low as 35.7 % (in Fe0.07Cu–N–C800). It can be observed that the content of Fe is an essential factor affecting the

FECO and, therefore, the efficiency of CO2ER products (Fig. 8a, Fig. S10). The FECO presents an upward trend with the increase of Fe content, especially in the low overpotential range of –1.1 ~ –1.4 V, increasing from 7.6~13.2 % (in Cu–N–C800) to 22.10~26.1 % (in Fe0.01Cu–N–C800). Further expanding the content of Fe leads to a significant improvement of the CO2ER, that is, 31.6~47.8 % and 43.0~48.5 % FECO were found in Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 and Fe0.13Cu–N–C800, respectively. Although the two catalysts, Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 and Fe0.13Cu–N–C800, present similar excellent FECO, the overpotential required in the former is smaller, indicating that the appropriate amount of Fe doping which in line with the Fe–Nx content, is more beneficial to improve the selectivity of the catalyst. Besides, the applied potential also significantly affects the activity and selectivity of CO2ER. The FECO decreases, and the FEH2 increases as the increase of the applied potential. The highest FECO of 47.8 % is observed at –1.2 V vs. Ag/AgCl in Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 catalyst.

sections.heading: 3.2.3. Catalyst stability analysis
sections.text: To study the stability of the catalyst, Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 was chosen as the research objective and was tested under the potential of –1.2 V vs. Ag/AgCl in CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (Fig. 8b). The current density can reach the platform within a short time and continuously maintain for 10 h (j = 1.06 mA cm–2), indicating excellent stability. The FECO decreases slightly during this period, from 47.8 % (2 h) to 37.6 % (10 h), probably due to the competition of HER and the partial peel off of the catalyst from the electrode. The morphology and composition present minor changes before and after electrolysis, as shown in the TEM and elemental mapping scheme (Fig. S11, Table S6).

sections.heading: 3.2.4. The performance evaluation
sections.text:
For each FexCu–N–C800 catalyst, an approximately linear increasing
trend of current density is obtained as the potential increases, as shown in Fig. S12a. Tafel plots were shown in the format of log(jco) versus the overpotential in the low potential range (Fig. S12b). The Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 catalyst exhibits the lowest slope of 250 mV dec–1, implying that it has the fastest kinetics for CO formation. During the CO2-to− CO process, the formation of *COOH, and then the desorption of *CO was considered to be the primary rate-determining step [36]. Since the Cu–N coordinate covalent bonds are unexpected for the fully occupied d-orbital (Cu◦) center, and the Cu–Nx moiety is spontaneously reduced to Cu◦ under strongly reducing condition, the metallic Cu particles are usually the actual active sites for Cu–N–C material [37]. The chronoamperometry result revealed that the catalyst with higher Fe doping has higher CO2ER activity, hinting that Fe–Nx site is effective for CO2 reduction to CO. When comparing the FE for the production of CO with those Cu/CuO related electrocatalysts, we got a consistent result, projecting the contribution of Fe-doping (Table S7). Moreover, the increase of Fe content directly increases the Fe–Nx sites and therefore reduces the overpotential (Fig. 8c).
On the calculation of the dispersion density of Cu NPs in carbon, the C: Cu atomic ratio increases as the increasing of Fe content, that is, 39.57 for Cu–N–C800, 53.3 for Fe0.01Cu–N–C800, 62.3 for Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 and 71.0 for Fe0.13Cu–N–C800. Due to the rich porous morphology they have, the Cu NPs could have full contact with the electrolyte through the carbon matrix, which has also been proved by the electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) test (Fig. 8d). It shows 9.4–10.7 Ω of charge transfer resistance (Rct) for each electrode (Table S8), closing to that of Cu–N–C800 (7.6 Ω). The slight increase of Rct is due to the decrease of Cu NPs with high electrical conductivity.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, we have synthesized series of Fe-Cu–BTT precursors by introducing the ferrous ion to microporous nitrogen-rich MOFs of Cu–BTT. Followed by a pyrolysis route, FexCu–N–C products with different content of Fe–Nx sites were obtained. Detailed characterization analyses indicate that Fe-doping induced the change of the structure, increase the BET surface area and the total pore volume, leading to a lower density of Cu NPs and higher content of Fe–Nx sites in the carbon matrix. As a result, an improvement in the production of CO was realized, of which the Fe0.07Cu–N–C800 exhibits the highest efficiency of 48.5 % for transferring CO2 to CO. This work illustrates the critical contribution of Fe–Nx sites on the CO2ER. The preparation of Fe–N–C material from direct pyrolization of Fe–BTT is under investigation in our group.
